findings.headline: Fire safety compliance gaps across corporate and school premises require Capital and Revenue reprofiling for remediation, with missing fire strategies and compartmentation issues

findings.matters: Fire safety is statutory compliance; failures create legal liability and reputational risk. The need to reprofile Capital and Revenue programmes indicates remediation costs were not fully provisioned and require reprioritisation.

findings.paper_title: au 2026 09 28 Performance and Risk Management - Appendix - Performance Risk Summary Report
findings.headline: External provider placement costs for looked-after children are rising due to National Minimum Wage and National Insurance increases, though the council achieved £12m in cost avoidance year-to-date
findings.detail: Rising placement costs for looked-after children are driven by increases in National Minimum Wage and employers' National Insurance contributions. findings.matters: A lender must understand volatile cost drivers in demand-led services; whilst cost avoidance demonstrates management action, placement costs remain structurally vulnerable to wage and National Insurance inflation.

findings.paper_title: au 2026 09 28 Worcestershire External Assurance Review - Appendix 4 - CIPFA Report on EFS Requests 2026-27 July 2025
findings.headline: Rising borrowing costs are directly worsening budget gaps for 70% of councils, not just affecting new lending.
findings.detail: 70% of councils report that financing costs, debt and Minimum Revenue Provision (MRP) pressures are secondary drivers of their budget distress. The paper notes this reflects sharp increases in borrowing costs following rises in interest rates from historic lows, and crucially states that these financing pressures are now directly contributing to councils' budget gaps. This is distinct from one-off borrowing rate changes and shows ongoing debt service costs are crowding out operational spending.
findings.matters: Interest rate rises are structural, not temporary. Higher debt service on existing debt reduces councils' ability to fund services and increases their reliance on EFS. A lender needs to know that the borrowing used to finance earlier EFS is now making future deficits worse.
findings.figures: 70% of councils reporting financing cost pressures
findings.quote: The same number of councils reported financing costs, debt and Minimum Revenue Provision (MRP) pressures. findings.matters: Many EFS councils' recovery strategies depend on delivering transformation savings to close budget gaps. If 70% have delivery risk, those recovery plans are likely to fail, meaning deficits will persist and further support will be needed.

findings.paper_title: au 2026 09 28 Worcestershire External Assurance Review - Appendix 4 - CIPFA Report on EFS Requests 2026-27 July 2025
findings.headline: 60% of councils are financing EFS through borrowing, creating a cycle of rising debt service and future deficits.
findings.detail: Rather than addressing underlying budget shortfalls through savings or service changes, the majority of EFS-receiving councils are using borrowing to bridge the gap. The paper explicitly states this is concerning because borrowing to cover budget gaps increases future financing costs, which then feed back into future budget gaps and further EFS requests. This turns a temporary problem into a structural debt service problem.
findings.matters: Borrowing to fund ongoing deficits worsens financial sustainability, not improves it. A lender needs to understand that 60% of EFS-receiving councils are increasing their debt burden to handle current spending, which reduces their ability to borrow for capital or to manage future shocks.
findings.figures: 60% of councils financing EFS through borrowing
findings.quote: 60% of councils are financing EFS through borrowing, which is concerning given the prevalence of financing pressures. Borrowing to address budget gaps increases future financing costs, contributing to a cycle of recurring EFS requests.

findings.paper_title: au 2026 09 28 Worcestershire External Assurance Review - Appendix 4 - CIPFA Report on EFS Requests 2026-27 July 2025
findings.headline: Councils requesting EFS in consecutive years face structural deficits that EFS is not solving.
findings.detail: The paper reports that councils which requested EFS in 2024/25 and 2025/26 are requesting it again in 2026/27. This pattern indicates that a significant subset of councils is still facing long-term financial challenges after receiving support, not temporary shortfalls. The paper notes that EFS is not a solution to long-standing structural challenges and that repeated requests by the same authorities demonstrate this is not working.
findings.matters: A lender assessing credit risk needs to know whether a council's deficit is temporary (can be bridged) or structural (will require ongoing support or restructuring). Repeated EFS requests show deficits are not being solved.
findings.figures: Councils requesting EFS in 2024/25, 2025/26 and again in 2026/27
findings.quote: Some authorities that requested EFS in 2024/25 and 2025/26 made requests again in 2026/27. This indicates that a significant subset of councils is still facing long-term financial challenges.

findings.paper_title: au 2026 09 28 2025-26 Interim External Auditor Report - Appendix 1 - Worcestershire CC AAR 2025-26 Interim draft - 15 September 2026
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation remains uncertain and is now creating an additional governance risk layer while the council manages multiple concurrent crises.
findings.detail: On 7 September 2026, the government announced it would review its local government reorganisation decision and paused implementation. Elections will proceed in May 2027 on existing council boundaries. The Council must manage this uncertainty while addressing financial distress, rapidly growing SEND costs, and transformation programmes that are failing to deliver at required scale. The auditor identifies residual risks including financial sustainability challenges that would be inherited by successor authorities, workforce capacity concerns during uncertainty, and the challenge of disaggregating services while maintaining safe delivery.
findings.matters: A lender assesses governance quality as an indicator of whether a council can navigate crises. The combination of financial distress, service pressures, inadequate transformation progress, and governance uncertainty compounds risk that organisational focus will be diverted from financial management or that key staff will leave.
findings.figures: Government review announced 7 September 2026; elections due May 2027 on existing council boundaries
findings.quote: The Council must therefore continue to deliver services and address its existing financial and service pressures while managing the uncertainty arising from the Government's review.

findings.paper_title: au 2026 09 28 2025-26 Interim External Auditor Report - Appendix 1 - Worcestershire CC AAR 2025-26 Interim draft - 15 September 2026
findings.headline: The council's breakeven outturn was achieved only through exceptional and unsustainable use of reserves and temporary government support, with reliance increasing.
findings.detail: The 2025/26 breakeven outturn required £33.6m of Exceptional Financial Support and £15.5m of reserves—approximately £0.5m more than budgeted. The 2026/27 budget continues to depend on up to £59.9m of EFS. The Council also applied £10.325m of capital receipts to reduce EFS-related borrowing against an original budget of £1.898m. Meanwhile, earmarked reserves fell from £93.7m to £75.8m and the General Fund balance remains below the Section 151 Officer's risk-assessed minimum of 5% of net budget.
findings.matters: Reserves are the first line of defence against unexpected cost shocks or revenue shortfalls. Depletion below prudent minimums combined with growing reliance on temporary government support that may not continue indefinitely signals increasing vulnerability and reduced financial resilience.

findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council has capacity to refinance existing borrowing or access new borrowing. Loss of headroom signals constrained borrowing capacity and rising refinancing risk at a time when DSG and service pressures are accelerating.

findings.headline: The Dedicated Schools Grant deficit has doubled in one year and is forecast to triple by 2028, with material uninsured liability after the statutory override expires.
findings.detail: The non-schools DSG deficit increased from £98.2m to £180.8m in a single year—an 83% increase. findings.figures: 12-month going concern assessment period
findings.quote: we have not identified any material uncertainties relating to events or conditions that, individually or collectively, may cast significant doubt on the Authority's ability to continue as a going concern

findings.paper_title: au 2026 09 28 Update on 2025-26 Financial Statements - Appendix 3 - Draft 2025-26 Audit Opinion (WCC)
findings.headline: Savings targets delivered but programme benefits forecast far below medium-term funding gaps
findings.detail: Savings and Transformation Programme delivered 2025/26 targets in full and established stronger governance with clearer ownership and benefit validation. However, programme remains at early stage with forecast benefits 'substantially below' medium-term funding gaps; council has not demonstrated ability to deliver at required scale.
findings.matters: One-off cost reductions achieved but do not address structural budget gap; demonstrated savings capability is materially insufficient for the scale of medium-term challenge.
findings.figures: Forecast benefits substantially below medium-term funding gaps
findings.quote: the programme remains at an early stage and its forecast benefits are substantially below the Council's medium-term funding gaps. The Council has not demonstrated that it can deliver recurrent, cashable savings at the scale and pace required to reduce its structural budget gap and reliance on EFS.

findings.paper_title: au 2026 09 28 Update on 2025-26 Financial Statements - Appendix 3 - Draft 2025-26 Audit Opinion (WCC)
findings.headline: Financial position unsustainable without continued emergency support; council using capital receipts to fund revenue borrowing
findings.detail: Council dependent on Exceptional Financial Support to balance 2026/27 budget. Reserves remain below prudent level; MTFP contains substantial unresolved funding gaps. Council is using capital receipts to reduce EFS-related borrowing, indicating reliance on unsustainable funding mechanisms.
findings.matters: Indicates structural budget problem requiring ongoing emergency government support; using capital resources for revenue costs is not sustainable and limits capital investment capacity.
findings.figures: Reserves below prudent level; substantial unresolved funding gaps in MTFP; capital receipts being deployed to reduce EFS-related borrowing
findings.quote: The Council remains dependent on Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) to balance its 2026/27 budget, reserves remain below the level assessed as prudent by the Section 151 Officer and its MTFP contains substantial unresolved funding gaps.

findings.paper_title: au 2026 09 28 Update on 2025-26 Financial Statements - Appendix 3 - Draft 2025-26 Audit Opinion (WCC)
findings.headline: 2025/26 breakeven achieved only through significant use of reserves; reserves now fall below prudent level
findings.detail: Breakeven outturn required substantial reserve drawdown and masked continuing service pressures in Adult Services and Children's Services. Post-year, reserves are assessed as being below the prudent level determined by the Section 151 Officer.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion reduces the council's capacity to absorb cost pressures or income shortfalls; underlying service costs remain unresolved.
findings.figures: Breakeven outturn achieved but requiring significant reserve use; reserves now below prudent level
findings.quote: The Council achieved a breakeven outturn for 2025/26 and delivered its savings target in full. However, the position required significant use of reserves and masked continuing pressures in Adult Services and Children's Services.

findings.paper_title: au 2026 09 28 Update on 2025-26 Financial Statements - Appendix 3 - Draft 2025-26 Audit Opinion (WCC)
findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant deficit nearly doubled in one year to £180.8m
findings.detail: DSG deficit grew from £98.2m at March 2025 to £180.8m at March 2026, increasing pressure on cashflow and capital financing. Auditors warn of potential material financial liability if government support is delayed or insufficient.
findings.matters: A quantified future liability of £180.8m requires ongoing government support and creates material uncertainty about the sustainability of education funding.
findings.quote: However, the deficit continues to grow, from £98.2m at 31 March 2025 to £180.8m at 31 March 2026, increasing pressure on the Council's cashflow and capital financing position

findings.paper_title: au 2026 09 28 Worcestershire External Assurance Review - Appendix 2 - EFS Action Plan Tracker September 2026
findings.headline: MRP policy review in 2023/24 delivered £10m savings over two years; further review to be completed by March 2027.
findings.detail: Recommendation 16 notes that 'A comprehensive review of MRP policy was completed in January 2024 by external experts, and changes were implemented in 2023/24, saving £10m over 2 years'. A further review will be completed 'ahead of LGR. It will be for each new authority to determine their own MRP policy'. This shows prior delivery of significant technical savings, though it also indicates the new councils will need to set their own policy from April 2028.
findings.matters: £10m in delivered MRP savings shows management has extracted value from technical financing decisions; however, the need for new councils to reset MRP policy post-LGR may create timing risk if new authorities adopt more conservative approaches.
findings.figures: £10m savings delivered over 2 years from 2023/24 MRP policy changes
findings.quote: A comprehensive review of MRP policy was completed in January 2024 by external experts, and changes were implemented in 2023/24, saving £10m over 2 years.

findings.paper_title: au 2026 09 28 Worcestershire External Assurance Review - Appendix 2 - EFS Action Plan Tracker September 2026
findings.headline: New finance system (TechOne) went live July 2026 with improved controls; implementation complete and on track.
findings.detail: Recommendation 5 (sequencing of system implementation) is marked 'Complete'. The system was 'launched in July 2026 and was sequenced to avoid financial year-end and budget setting'. System features include better visibility of spending, stronger approval processes, and improved forecasting. Training was delivered to all users in July 2026.
findings.matters: System improvements provide foundation for strengthened financial control going forward; completion of implementation removes execution risk from the finance function's effectiveness.
findings.figures: System went live July 2026; training completed July 2026
findings.quote: The new finance system was launched in July 2026 and was sequenced to avoid financial year-end and budget setting. We have used the wider finance team flexibly during this period to respond to peaks and pressures caused by system implementation.

findings.paper_title: au 2026 09 28 Worcestershire External Assurance Review - Appendix 2 - EFS Action Plan Tracker September 2026
findings.headline: Financial forecasting accuracy is strong: 2025/26 outturn was 0.4% off Q3 forecast.
findings.detail: Recommendation 9 (on monthly forecasting discipline) includes this statement: 'We can stand behind the accuracy of our in-year forecasting, with 2025/26 outturn moving from Q3 forecast by just 0.4% of Net budget, and from Q2 by under 1.6%'. This is unusual precision and indicates financial management capability is present, even under stress.
findings.matters: For a council in EFS, accurate forecasting is a critical control that allows early intervention on overspends. This data suggests management has visibility and control of budget execution.
findings.figures: 0.4% variance from Q3 forecast to outturn (2025/26); under 1.6% variance from Q2 forecast
findings.quote: We can stand behind the accuracy of our in-year forecasting, with 2025/26 outturn moving from Q3 forecast by just 0.4% of Net budget, and from Q2 by under 1.6%.

findings.paper_title: au 2026 09 28 Worcestershire External Assurance Review - Appendix 2 - EFS Action Plan Tracker September 2026
findings.headline: Multiple demand-led service transformations are rated CIPFA risk 9 (highest urgency), including Children's, Adults and SEND services.
findings.detail: Recommendations 17–21 address Children's Services placements, SEND financial planning, and Adult Social Care rebalancing. All are rated CIPFA 9, indicating high-urgency, high-risk delivery. Children's Services has implemented Families First model (deployed ahead of national schedule) and multi-disciplinary teams; Adults Services is undertaking specialist reviews via PeopleToo on supported living and transitions (due September/October 2026). These are foundational to closing the budget gap but each carries transformation risk.
findings.matters: These services are cost-drivers in the budget; failure to deliver transformation would force additional savings from elsewhere or trigger reserve drawdown, directly affecting EFS exit feasibility.
findings.figures: 25% increase in Foster Carers over last 24 months; 20% increase in Family Hub attendances over last 12 months; £200k cost reduction from 2 CHC cases in July 2026
findings.quote: We are one of only two authorities (out of 14) in the region to have implemented Families First (which delivers early help, family support and safeguarding services, designed to provide the right help at the right time and reduce the need for children to enter more intensive statutory services).

findings.paper_title: au 2026 09 28 Worcestershire External Assurance Review - Appendix 2 - EFS Action Plan Tracker September 2026
findings.headline: DSG deficit recovery plan leaves a 10% unfunded gap even if High Needs Stability Grant is received.
findings.detail: Recommendation 10 requires a plan for covering historic and future DSG deficits. The council states it is 'working with the Society of County Treasurers to understand the implications to authorities that may have significant residual gaps, once the High Needs Stability Grant is received'. It will then 'continue to build upon mitigations via the High Needs Deficit Management Plan with a focus on the remaining 10% deficit should we be granted the High Needs Stability Grant'. This indicates a structured, unfunded liability even in the best case (grant receipt).
findings.matters: A 10% DSG deficit that remains unfunded is a balance sheet liability that reduces the council's financial resilience and must be absorbed through future savings or reserves drawdown.
findings.figures: Remaining 10% deficit even if High Needs Stability Grant received
findings.quote: we continue to build upon mitigations via the High Needs Deficit Management Plan with a focus on the remaining 10% deficit should we be granted the High Needs Stability Grant.

findings.paper_title: au 2026 09 28 Worcestershire External Assurance Review - Appendix 2 - EFS Action Plan Tracker September 2026
findings.headline: Savings plans are behind schedule and described as requiring 'urgent need to accelerate', rated CIPFA risk 9.
findings.detail: Recommendation 11 explicitly states there is an 'urgent need to accelerate the development of fully costed, timebound savings plans'. The status is 'In Progress' with no completion date before October 2026. The response indicates savings proposals are only now being formed (from June 2026) with scrutiny review scheduled October/December 2026. The plan must include sensitivity analysis for 10%, 25% and 50% underdelivery, suggesting management concern about delivery risk.
findings.matters: Savings plans are the mechanism for EFS exit; if they are not yet fully costed or scheduled for only October review, there is material delivery risk to the exit strategy.
findings.figures: Sensitivity analysis required for 10%, 25% and 50% underdelivery scenarios; CIPFA risk rating 9
findings.quote: There is an urgent need to accelerate the development of fully costed, timebound savings plans with clear ownership, delivery milestones and risk rated trajectories, supported by strengthened programme management and monthly reporting to ensure grip, pace and early intervention.

findings.paper_title: au 2026 09 28 Worcestershire External Assurance Review - Appendix 2 - EFS Action Plan Tracker September 2026
findings.headline: Council's EFS exit plan is due in December 2026 but timeline is compressed by local government reorganisation scheduled for April 2028.
findings.detail: Recommendation 12 requires a clear and credible EFS exit plan showing how the council will achieve a sustainable financial position and eliminate the need for EFS. The council's response indicates that from 2027/28 'EFS exit plans must be part of LGR plans and the financial strategy of the two new Worcestershire councils'. This creates a compressed timeline: the exit plan must be designed by December 2026 and implemented into a new council structure by April 2028, with no clear contingency if LGR is delayed.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know the exit strategy is realistic and funded, not dependent on uncertain organisational changes that could slip.
findings.figures: EFS exit plan due December 2026; LGR completion April 2028; less than 16 months to implementation
findings.quote: From 2027/28, EFS exit plans must be part of LGR plans and the financial strategy of the two new Worcestershire councils.

findings.paper_title: au 2026 09 28 Treasury Management Update Quarter 1
findings.headline: Council's investment portfolio outperformed benchmark by 45 basis points in Q1, yielding 4.18% against 3.73% target.
findings.detail: Worcestershire achieved gross investment income of £541k in the first three months of 2026-27 on average holdings of £51.882m. Portfolio yield of 4.18% exceeded the 7-day SONIA benchmark of 3.73%. Investments are diversified across Money Market Funds (£41m), Bond Funds (£10m), Banks (£1m), maintaining security while capturing available yield.
findings.matters: Effective treasury management on the investment side contributes to revenue, though this is modest relative to the council's overall debt servicing costs.
findings.figures: Average holdings £51.882m, yield 4.18% vs benchmark 3.73%, gross income £541k for Q1
findings.quote: the average investment portfolio yield for the first 3 months of the year is 4.18% against a benchmark (7-day SONIA) of 3.73%. Gross income from treasury investments for the first 3 months of the financial year was £541k.

findings.paper_title: au 2026 09 28 Treasury Management Update Quarter 1
findings.headline: Average rate on outstanding debt increased from 3.81% to 4.07% in the first quarter, a rise of 26 basis points.
findings.detail: The council's weighted average borrowing rate increased during Q1 2026-27 from 3.81% at 31 March to 4.07% at 30 June. This 26bp rise reflects both market conditions and the composition of new borrowing and maturing debt in the quarter. Given the forecast £930.3m external debt position and rising rate outlook, this deterioration materially increases the council's revenue burden.
findings.matters: Rising debt costs increase revenue pressure and reduce financial flexibility; the impact is material given the scale of additional borrowing forecast.
findings.figures: Average borrowing rate 3.81% (31 March 2026) to 4.07% (30 June 2026); total external debt £713.9m
findings.quote: There was £713.9m of debt outstanding on 30 June 2026 (£716.9m at 31 March 2026) at an average rate of 4.07% (3.81% at 31 March 2026)

findings.paper_title: au 2026 09 28 Treasury Management Update Quarter 1
findings.headline: Council is exceeding agreed prudential limits for short-term debt maturity, with 29.74% of debt maturing within one year against a limit of 0-25%.
findings.detail: Of £713.9m total external debt as at 30 June 2026, £212.3m (29.74%) is maturing within one year, exceeding the approved limit of 0-25% for that band. The council acknowledges this breach and expects to seek Cabinet approval to modify the percentage thresholds. The council justifies this as tactical, reflecting expectations that interest rates will fall and that grant income will allow early repayment of short-term borrowing.
findings.matters: Breach of prudential limits indicates the council is accepting maturity and liquidity risk, and requires regulatory approval to address.
findings.figures: £212.3m of £713.9m total external debt (29.74%) maturing within 1 year, against approved limit of 0-25%
findings.quote: the Council is currently exceeded the agreed limits for under 12 months maturity.

findings.paper_title: au 2026 09 28 Treasury Management Update Quarter 1
findings.headline: External debt including DSG is forecast to reach £930.3m by March 2027, up £213.5m in a single year, driven by borrowing to fund the DSG deficit.
findings.detail: The council is using short-term borrowing to fund its DSG deficit, forecast to grow total external debt from £716.8m to £930.3m between 2025-26 and 2026-27. This forecast excludes an expected but unconfirmed £162m High Needs Stability Grant due in Autumn 2026, which is assumed necessary to improve cash position. If the grant is not received, the council will face immediate pressure on reserves and liquidity.
findings.matters: Lenders need to understand whether a council can sustain rapid debt growth and whether its strategy is contingent on funding that may not materialise.
findings.figures: External debt including DSG: £716.8m (2025-26 actual) to £930.3m (2026-27 forecast), increase of £213.5m; High Needs Stability Grant of c£162m expected but not confirmed Autumn 2026
findings.quote: Based on the latest Capital Programme update, the forecast for 31 March 2027 is £930.3m.

findings.paper_title: au 2026 09 28 Update on 2025-26 Financial Statements - Appendix 5 - Draft 2025-26 Audit Findings Report (WCC)
findings.headline: VAT debtor of £1.7m written off after HMRC confirmed non-recoverability post-accounts preparation; recorded as unadjusted misstatement.
findings.detail: During the audit, the council identified that a VAT debtor of £1.7m that had been included in the draft financial statements is not recoverable. HMRC confirmed this after the accounts had been prepared. The auditor recorded this as an unadjusted misstatement but management has elected not to adjust the accounts, considering the item not material. This leaves the balance sheet overstated at the year-end date.
findings.matters: The VAT recovery represents 5.5% of the council's total adjusted VAT position and material cash was expected. Its loss affects the council's liquidity position and should have been anticipated earlier. The fact that it was not suggests either poor financial controls or late discovery of a known issue.
findings.figures: £1.7m VAT debtor written off; management assessment: not material
findings.quote: During our testing of VAT we noted a balance of £1.7m which had been included as a Debtor. However, since the preparation of the financial statements, HMRC have confirmed that this amount will not be recoverable

findings.paper_title: au 2026 09 28 Update on 2025-26 Financial Statements - Appendix 5 - Draft 2025-26 Audit Findings Report (WCC)
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation scheduled for 1 April 2028 will replace Worcestershire's seven existing councils with two unitary authorities, but going concern basis remains appropriate.
findings.detail: The Government announced on 16 July 2026 that Worcestershire's seven existing county, city, district and borough councils will be replaced by two new unitary councils from 1 April 2028. The council assumes that all functions, assets and liabilities of Worcestershire County Council will be transferred to the newly created authorities. The auditor concluded that because the council's functions will continue regardless of the structural decision, the going concern basis of accounting remains appropriate for the 2025/26 accounts. However, the reorganisation is flagged in an Emphasis of Matter paragraph in the audit report.
findings.matters: A structural reorganisation on this scale creates uncertainty about future service continuity, asset handling, and the stability of the council's financial position in the near to medium term. A lender needs to understand whether the reorganisation creates refinancing risk or affects the counterparty with whom they lent.
findings.figures: Reorganisation date: 1 April 2028; current position: 7 councils to become 2 unitary authorities
findings.quote: As the functions of the County Council will continue regardless of the decision, it is appropriate for the 2025-26 accounts to be prepared on a going concern basis.

findings.paper_title: au 2026 09 28 Update on 2025-26 Financial Statements - Appendix 5 - Draft 2025-26 Audit Findings Report (WCC)
findings.headline: Lease arrangement control failure: one lease omitted from IFRS 16 lease population for six years and incorrectly classified as freehold, only identified during 2025/26 closedown.
findings.detail: During 2025/26, the council identified through a completeness review that a lease arrangement had been omitted from its IFRS 16 lease accounting population for six years and had been incorrectly classified as a freehold asset. This was not identified through the council's normal controls and only came to light through a retrospective completeness review undertaken as part of year-end closedown. The auditor has recommended strengthening controls over the identification and ongoing review of lease arrangements.
findings.matters: A six-year control failure in lease identification suggests significant gaps in the council's asset management processes. IFRS 16 lease liabilities affect the council's apparent leverage and borrowing ratios. The fact that no preventive control caught this earlier indicates the control environment's weakness.
findings.figures: One lease arrangement omitted for six years until identified in 2025/26 closedown
findings.quote: Controls over the identification and completeness of lease arrangements were not effective in identifying one lease arrangement which was omitted from the Council's IFRS 16 lease population and incorrectly classified as a freehold asset for six years. The omission was only identified through a completeness review undertaken as part of the 2025/26 closedown process.

findings.paper_title: au 2026 09 28 Update on 2025-26 Financial Statements - Appendix 5 - Draft 2025-26 Audit Findings Report (WCC)
findings.headline: Land and building valuations decreased by £27.5m (5.4%) to £485.1m; Energy from Waste plant decreased by £0.8m to £94.2m.
findings.detail: The valuation of land and buildings (including schools and libraries) fell from £512.6m in 2024/25 to £485.1m in 2025/26, a decrease of £27.5m. The Energy from Waste plant asset decreased from £95.0m to £94.2m, a 0.8% fall. Both movements reflect indexation and revaluation exercises. The council revalued 36% of total assets during 2025/26 and applied indexation (a new requirement under the 2025/26 CIPFA Code) to £293.4m of assets (60% of land and buildings). The auditor found no material adjustments were required.
findings.matters: A substantial decline in asset valuations reduces the council's balance sheet asset base and can affect borrowing capacity calculations that reference asset backing. The scale of the movement (£27.5m on a £485m base) is material and warrants understanding whether it reflects market movements or valuation methodology changes.
findings.figures: L&B: £512.6m (2024/25) to £485.1m (2025/26), decrease £27.5m; EfW: £95.0m to £94.2m, decrease £0.8m (0.8%); indexation applied to £293.4m (60% of land and buildings)
findings.quote: The total year-end valuation of land and buildings was £485.1 million, a net decrease of £27.5 million from 2024/25 (£512.6 million)... The total year-end valuation of the Energy from Waste Plant was £94.2 million, representing a decrease of £0.8 million (0.8%) from the 2024/25 valuation of £95.0 million.

findings.paper_title: au 2026 09 28 Update on 2025-26 Financial Statements - Appendix 5 - Draft 2025-26 Audit Findings Report (WCC)
findings.headline: Control weaknesses persist in journal authorization, with the ledger system permitting posters to self-authorise journals, a finding retained from prior audits.
findings.detail: The auditor notes that there is no automatic control requiring all journals to be authorised and that manual controls do not cover all journals, increasing the risk of misstatement. Specifically, posters can self-authorise their journals. The auditor notes this is 'a limitation of the ledger system and therefore not easily in the control of management' and has kept open prior-year recommendations in respect of this matter. This remains a significant risk in the management override control area, though no material misstatement was identified.
findings.matters: Journal controls are a first-line defence against fraud and error. Persistent system-level control gaps in such a critical area indicate that management and the council have accepted this risk rather than resolved it, and suggest reliance on detective controls (audit) rather than preventive controls.
findings.figures: Ongoing issue identified in current year audit; prior year recommendation kept open
findings.quote: We note that there is no automatic control that requires all journals to be authorised and that manual controls do not cover all journals. This increases the risk of misstatement... we have kept open our prior year recommendations in respect of this matter.

findings.paper_title: au 2026 09 28 Update on 2025-26 Financial Statements - Appendix 5 - Draft 2025-26 Audit Findings Report (WCC)
findings.headline: Section 106 developer contributions totalling £2.3m held in creditors include historic balances beyond the contractual spend deadline with no evidence of commitment.
findings.detail: The council holds £2.3m in Section 106 developer contributions within grants received in advance. Of this, £1.2m relates to accrued interest with no present obligation to repay, and £1.0m comprises historic balances with insufficient supporting evidence to demonstrate they represent valid obligations. The spend deadlines on these contributions have expired. Management has confirmed an intention to release these balances to revenue in 2026/27, but the auditor has recorded this as an unadjusted misstatement, indicating it remains unresolved.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council is correctly accounting for its actual liabilities. Overstated creditors and understated income suggest either poor financial controls or a mischaracterization of liabilities. Developer contributions can create reputational and legal risk if repayment obligations are not managed correctly.
findings.figures: £2.3m total Section 106 balances; £1.2m accrued interest; £1.0m historic balances without supporting evidence
findings.quote: The £1.2m balance, relating to accrued interest, does not meet the definition of a provision or liability under the CIPFA Code, as there is no present obligation and outflow is not probable. The remaining £1.0m comprises historic balances with insufficient supporting evidence to demonstrate they represent valid obligations

findings.paper_title: au 2026 09 28 Update on 2025-26 Financial Statements - Appendix 5 - Draft 2025-26 Audit Findings Report (WCC)
findings.headline: Minimum Revenue Provision charge increased by £1.2m (7%) to £18.4m, driven by capitalisation direction treatment of Exceptional Financial Support, with further increases expected.
findings.detail: The council's MRP charge (the amount charged to revenue to repay capital financed by borrowing) increased by £1.2m from 2024/25 to £18.4m in 2025/26. This increase is driven by the £33.6m Exceptional Financial Support treated as a capitalisation direction, which increases the capital financing requirement and therefore the annual MRP charge. Because the EFS is unfinanced from capital resources, it increases the council's CFR (capital financing requirement) and therefore the MRP charge required in future years over the 20-year repayment period.
findings.matters: The MRP charge is a fixed, unavoidable revenue cost that reduces the council's ability to fund other services. A 7% year-on-year increase signals deteriorating budget headroom and constrains future financial flexibility.
findings.quote: The Authority received EFS of £33.6m in 2025/26, granted via a capitalisation direction from MHCLG... Where this is unfinanced from capital resources (grant or capital receipts), it increases the Authority's CFR and therefore increases the MRP charge required in future.

findings.paper_title: au 2026 09 28 Update on 2025-26 Financial Statements - Appendix 5 - Draft 2025-26 Audit Findings Report (WCC)
findings.headline: Value for money significant weaknesses in financial sustainability and economy/efficiency arrangements remain, with statutory recommendation carried forward from prior year.
findings.detail: The auditor's value-for-money assessment found significant weaknesses in the council's arrangements for financial sustainability and improving economy, efficiency and effectiveness. Despite the council making progress in addressing prior findings, further action is required. The statutory recommendation issued in November 2025 remains in progress and has not been fully implemented; the auditor has retained four key recommendations from 2024/25 (two on financial sustainability, two on economy/efficiency).
findings.matters: Unresolved value-for-money recommendations indicate systemic issues in the council's approach to financial management and resource efficiency, directly relevant to its ability to maintain financial stability and meet future demands.
findings.figures: One statutory recommendation not yet fully implemented; four key recommendations retained from 2024/25
findings.quote: Significant weaknesses remain in the Council's arrangements for financial sustainability and improving economy, efficiency and effectiveness. While the Council has made progress in addressing our previous findings, further action is required.

findings.paper_title: au 2026 09 28 Update on 2025-26 Financial Statements - Appendix 5 - Draft 2025-26 Audit Findings Report (WCC)
findings.headline: Exceptional Financial Support of £33.6m represents a structural increase to the council's debt position, not a one-off adjustment.
findings.detail: The council received £33.6m of Exceptional Financial Support from the Ministry of Housing, Communities, and Local Government for 2025/26, via a capitalisation direction. The auditor explicitly notes that this support 'represents a structural increase to the Authority's debt position rather than a one-off adjustment, and increases the annual MRP charge going forward.' The capitalisation direction requires MRP to be charged over no more than 20 years, creating an ongoing revenue commitment.
findings.matters: A lender assessing the council's creditworthiness needs to understand whether support is temporary or has locked in long-term costs. A structural debt increase affects future borrowing capacity and budget flexibility.
findings.figures: £33.6m for 2025/26; MRP charge of £18.4m in 2025/26 (up £1.2m from prior year); charges to continue for up to 20 years
findings.quote: Members should be aware that reliance on EFS represents a structural increase to the Authority's debt position rather than a one-off adjustment, and increases the annual MRP charge going forward.

findings.paper_title: au 2026 09 28 Update on 2025-26 Financial Statements - Appendix 6 - Draft 2025-26 Audit Findings Report (WPF)
findings.headline: Pension Schemes Act 2026 enacted to address Virgin Media judgment uncertainty on historic pension scheme amendments, with ongoing discussions with actuaries on LGPS implications.
findings.detail: The Court of Appeal judgment in Virgin Media Ltd v NTL Pension Trustees II Ltd raised uncertainty about pension scheme amendments where contemporaneous actuarial confirmation could not be evidenced. The Pension Schemes Act 2026 (Royal Assent 29 April 2026) introduced retrospective confirmation legislation. Government guidance indicates LGPS schemes are expected to have met statutory requirements with no material impact anticipated, but the fund is continuing discussions with actuary Hymans Robertson to confirm the position.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether historic pension liabilities could be materially re-assessed; while the government signal suggests LGPS is not affected, ongoing monitoring with actuaries indicates uncertainty remains pending confirmation.
findings.figures: No material impact currently expected; discussions ongoing with Hymans Robertson, fund actuary.
findings.quote: the Government, supported by guidance from The Pensions Regulator and the Financial Reporting Council, has indicated that public service pension schemes, including the LGPS, are expected to have met the relevant statutory requirements and therefore no changes to LGPS benefits or liabilities are currently expected.

findings.paper_title: au 2026 09 28 Update on 2025-26 Financial Statements - Appendix 6 - Draft 2025-26 Audit Findings Report (WPF)
findings.headline: Admitted body pension contributions fell 95% from £11.0m to £0.6m in a single year due to Worcestershire Children's First transfer and housing association departures.
findings.detail: The fund disclosed a significant reduction in admitted body contributions from £11.0 million to £0.6 million, reflecting structural changes: the Worcestershire Children's First transfer and exits of housing association employers. This represents a material change in the contribution income profile and employer base.
findings.matters: A council finance director would need to understand whether this represents a temporary one-off (the Children's First transfer) or an ongoing attrition of admitted bodies that could affect future contribution receipts and funding ratios; a lender would assess whether this signals employer covenant weakening.
findings.figures: Admitted body contributions reduced from £11.0 million to £0.6 million.
findings.quote: the movement reflected both the Worcestershire Children's First transfer and housing association exits during the year

findings.paper_title: au 2026 09 28 Update on 2025-26 Financial Statements - Appendix 6 - Draft 2025-26 Audit Findings Report (WPF)
findings.headline: Prior-year IT control recommendations from 2020/21 remain outstanding six years later, with four specific deficiencies unresolved.
findings.detail: Four recommendations from the 2020/21 IT audit remain outstanding: user access reviews are only occasional rather than systematic; there is no retained documentation for successful batch jobs in the E5 system; there is a lack of proactive service provider assurance report review; and Altair admin rights and password policy issues have been only partially addressed with compensating controls rather than system fixes.
findings.matters: A lender or finance director would care that critical IT control recommendations from six years ago remain unresolved, suggesting either capability gaps or insufficient prioritisation of control improvements in a system managing £4.5 billion in assets.

findings.paper_title: 7 Budget Monitoring P3 Final
findings.headline: The council explicitly acknowledged the risk of a Section 114 notice (formal declaration of financial crisis) and states that avoiding it requires a "clear and significant programme of activities".
findings.detail: Section 114 is a formal declaration by the Chief Financial Officer that projected income is insufficient to cover anticipated spending and the council cannot set or maintain a balanced budget. The council states that "a clear and significant programme of activities is required in order to avoid the position where a Section 114 notice needs to be issued" but acknowledges it is "too early in the process to have a robust plan that can be included in the MTFP". This signals unresolved financial instability and plan-less recovery.
findings.matters: A Section 114 notice is among the most severe financial warnings a council can issue. Its explicit mention signals to lenders that the council is aware it is at financial risk and that recovery plans are not yet concrete or complete.

findings.paper_title: 7 Budget Monitoring P3 Final

This deficit sits on the balance sheet under statutory override until March 2028, but creates real cash pressure and borrowing costs. The auditors have issued a Statutory Recommendation on the severity of this position.
findings.matters: The deficit is large, growing, and will impact the council's financial viability when the statutory override ends in March 2028. Until then it creates cash drag requiring additional borrowing (costing c£5m this year). The 10% the council must fund after the override ends could be £40.6m, threatening reserves.
findings.figures: £180.8m opening deficit; £104.1m 2026/27 overspend; £284.9m forecast before grant; £122.2m forecast after £162.7m grant; £162.7m expected November 2026; £5m additional borrowing cost this year; £40.6m potential unfunded portion from March 2028

findings.paper_title: 7 Budget Monitoring P3 Final

findings.detail: Worcestershire was granted a Capitalisation Directive as Exceptional Financial Support, allowing it to borrow £59.9m for day-to-day revenue spending rather than capital investment. This is not additional cash but permission to borrow, with repayment of principal and interest due over 20 years. The council could not set a balanced budget without this support.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know that the council's budget only works with government permission to borrow for revenue, not income. The interest and repayment costs will be embedded in future years' budgets, reducing financial flexibility.

findings.paper_title: 2026 02 26 Budget - Appendix 4 - Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: Council must take unprecedented short-term borrowing to cover underfunded SEND High Needs until March 2028
findings.detail: The Government has not funded SEND High Needs adequately through the Dedicated Schools Grant, forcing Worcestershire into additional short-term borrowing of £127.6m in 2026/27, rising to £160.7m in 2027/28. The council is losing approximately £7.5m annually in treasury management income as a result. The Government will not take responsibility for cumulative deficits until March 2028, leaving the council to bridge the gap with interest-bearing debt—effectively providing an interest-free loan to the Department for Education. The CFO explicitly states this would have prevented them meeting balanced budget requirements in 2025/26 without this shortfall.
findings.matters: This forces the council into substantial short-term borrowing that must be refinanced multiple times before 2028, creating cumulative interest costs and cash-flow volatility. The lack of clarity on how government will manage historic deficits after March 2028 leaves the council's medium-term sustainability uncertain.
findings.figures: £7.5m annual treasury income loss; £93.6m DSG borrowing 2025/26; £127.6m in 2026/27; £160.7m in 2027/28; debt including DSG projected to reach £1,248.3m by March 2028
findings.quote: This means that the cumulative impact is growing exponentially and the effect on sustainability is ever increasing, due to lost interest income and higher borrowing costs, with councils effectively providing an interest-free loan to the Department for Education.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4 - Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27

This reflects the growing debt burden from both capital expenditure and DSG cashflowing. The 2027/28 increase occurs just as the DSG deficit pressure reaches its peak.
findings.matters: A rising ratio of financing costs to revenue shows an increasing share of the council's income committed to debt service, constraining flexibility for service spending. The uptick in 2027/28 coincides with maximum DSG pressure and capital expenditure commitments.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4 - Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: PWLB borrowing rates remain elevated despite base rate cuts; 50-year loans peaked at 6.14%
findings.detail: Despite the Bank of England reducing base rate from 4.50% to 3.75% during 2025, Public Works Loan Board rates for longer-term borrowing have remained stubbornly high. The 50-year rate peaked at 6.14% and is forecast to remain above 5% through the forecast period. This constrains the council's borrowing options, particularly for long-term funding.
findings.matters: A borrowing council facing multiple demands (capital programme, DSG deficit, maturing debt) benefits from falling rates. Persistent elevation in PWLB rates raises the cost of meeting those demands, especially for the 25+ year maturities often used in local authority borrowing.

findings.paper_title: 2026 02 26 Updated Budget Report 2026-27

findings.paper_title: 2026 02 26 Updated Budget Report 2026-27
findings.headline: £59.933 million unfunded budget gap requires government capitalisation directive approval to set a balanced budget

findings.paper_title: 2026 02 26 Updated Section 25 Report - 2026-27
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation transition costs potentially exceeding £20 million must be funded by all seven authorities with no national funding, adding pressure during peak financial constraint
findings.detail: Worcestershire is moving toward a single unitary authority (vesting April 2028) following LGR proposals submitted by the seven local authorities in November 2025. Experience from other council mergers suggests transition costs could exceed £20 million. Government has explicitly stated there will be no national funding for these costs, requiring all seven authorities to jointly fund and manage them. The S151 Officer notes this 'will remain a risk going into 2026/27 that will need to be carefully monitored' and that 'all 7 councils in the area will need to work together effectively to jointly contribute and manage the required transition costs as a system.'
findings.matters: Unfunded transition costs of this scale, to be borne during a period of peak financial stress and in a period when the council cannot balance its budget, represent a significant contingent liability and source of additional financial pressure during the critical 2026-28 period.
findings.figures: Transition costs potentially exceeding £20 million; to be funded collectively by 7 authorities; no national funding available; LGR vesting date April 2028

findings.paper_title: 2026 02 26 Updated Section 25 Report - 2026-27
findings.headline: Chronic overspends in Children's and Adult Social Care placements show worsening pattern despite management action: £6.2m (2024/25) following £19.1m underlying deficit (2023/24)

findings.matters: A multi-year pattern of unmanaged social care demand growth, masked by one-off reserves and government grants, indicates structural cost pressures the council cannot control, making long-term financial sustainability dependent on service redesign or demand reduction the council has not yet achieved.

findings.paper_title: 2026 02 26 Updated Section 25 Report - 2026-27
findings.headline: Only £8.945 million in planned recurrent savings for 2026/27, described by the S151 Officer as 'nowhere near enough' for an organisation of this size
findings.detail: The council has identified just £8.945 million in savings for 2026/27. The Chief Financial Officer explicitly states this is inadequate: 'as £8.945 million is nowhere near enough for an organisation of this size, transformation is the only viable route to deliver savings at the scale and speed required.' This follows a pattern: £12.5 million in 2025/26 and £8.9 million in 2026/27. The council is working with PwC on a transformation plan to close the gap, but delivery is uncertain against mounting LGR implementation commitments.
findings.matters: Acknowledged insufficiency of planned recurrent savings means the budget gap remains unresolved; reliance on 'transformation' (not yet specified) and one-off central government support rather than structural cost control.
findings.figures: £8.945 million planned savings for 2026/27; £12.5 million in 2025/26; £19.1 million overspend before mitigations in 2023/24
findings.quote: as £8.945 million is nowhere near enough for an organisation of this size, and the nature of the challenges faced by the council, transformation is the only viable route to deliver savings at the scale and speed required

findings.paper_title: 2026 02 26 Updated Section 25 Report - 2026-27
findings.headline: 2025/26 forecast position is already £2.2 million worse than budgeted, requiring £17.2 million reserves drawdown plus £33.6 million EFS
findings.detail: At Q3 2025/26, the council is forecasting a breakeven position only after using £2.2 million more reserves than the budgeted £15 million, plus £33.6 million of Exceptional Financial Support. Services show a £13.3 million overspend, partially offset by £11.1 million in corporate savings (chiefly reduced borrowing costs). This demonstrates inability to deliver even within adjusted forecasts mid-year.
findings.matters: An in-year forecast that slips by £2.2 million in just nine months, requiring emergency central government support to avoid a Section 114 notice, shows severe expenditure control problems.
findings.figures: £2.2 million additional overspend vs budget; £17.2 million reserves use (vs £15 million budgeted); £33.6 million EFS; £13.3 million services overspend
findings.quote: At Quarter 3 (December) 2025/26, the Council is forecasting an indicative breakeven position after use of £17.2 million of reserves (£2.2 million more than the budgeted £15 million due to overspends in Adult and Children's Services) and a further £33.6 million of Exceptional Financial Support.

findings.paper_title: 2026 02 26 Updated Section 25 Report - 2026-27
findings.headline: £194.1 million Special Educational Needs deficit is hidden from the balance sheet and crystallises when statutory override expires March 2028
findings.detail: The council holds approximately £194.1 million of accumulated unfunded SEND expenditure by March 2026, masked by a temporary statutory override that allows it to be excluded from accounts. This override expires March 2028. If government does not assume responsibility for funding SEND or approve a mechanism for addressing the legacy deficit by then, councils will be forced to recognise these liabilities. The government has announced a High Needs Stability Grant (to pay 90% of deficits in Autumn 2026), but the mechanism for the remaining debt and a cumulative national deficit of approximately £14 billion remains unresolved.
findings.matters: This is a latent liability of exceptional size that will either require massive additional revenue funding, further borrowing capacity, or a Section 114 notice if not resolved by central government; it represents the council's single largest financial risk.
findings.figures: £194.1 million accumulated SEND deficit by March 2026; £14 billion cumulative national deficit by March 2028; any local borrowing solution estimated at £7.5 million annually in revenue costs
findings.quote: By March 2026, Worcestershire County Council is forecast to hold approximately £194.1 million of additional debt arising from unfunded expenditure on statutory Special Educational Needs and Disabilities (SEND) services over several years. This represents the Council's most significant financial risk.

findings.paper_title: 2026 02 26 Updated Section 25 Report - 2026-27
findings.headline: Council cannot set a balanced budget without Exceptional Financial Support and council tax flexibility above referendum limits
findings.detail: The council faces a £59.933 million budget gap for 2026/27 after the Final Local Government Settlement. This is being bridged by approved council tax flexibility of 4% (worth £14.4 million per year) and a requested Capitalisation Direction as part of the EFS framework. The Section 151 Officer has made formal submissions to MHCLG requesting both.
findings.matters: A council unable to set a lawful budget without government-granted dispensations is a fundamental credit risk to any lender; the reliance on central government discretion removes financial autonomy.
findings.figures: £59.933 million budget gap; 4% council tax flexibility granted worth £14.4 million per year (£43.2 million over MTFP period); Capitalisation Direction requested
findings.quote: the Council's financial position is critical, given its inability since 2025/26 to set a balanced Revenue Budget without reliance upon Exceptional Financial Support (EFS)

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4 - Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: Capital expenditure is forecast to increase 100% over five years (£97m in 2024/25 to £141.7m by 2028/29), placing sustained pressure on borrowing and MRP charges.
findings.detail: Table 3 shows capital expenditure increasing from £97.0m (2024/25 actual) to a peak of £193.8m (2026/27), then moderating to £141.7m (2028/29). The increase is driven by approved capital programmes but, combined with the DSG borrowing need, creates multiple years of elevated debt and MRP costs that will flow into revenue budgets for decades.
findings.matters: Sustained high capital expenditure locks the council into rising financing costs. MRP will become a larger revenue charge as the CFR grows. A lender needs to see that the council can sustain both the capital ambition and the resulting debt servicing obligations from within its operating budget.
findings.figures: Capital expenditure 2024/25: £97.0m; 2026/27 peak: £193.8m; net financing need 2026/27: £50.3m

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4 - Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: Mercia Waste loan facility has been extended by 5 years with adjusted terms, and the council is exposed to refinancing risk when the extension ends in January 2029.
findings.detail: The council and Herefordshire jointly provided £92m (WCC's share, as at 31 March 2024) in financing for an Energy from Waste PFI with Mercia Waste. In 2024, they agreed to extend the contract by 5 years to January 2029 and reduce the bullet repayment amount from circa £128m to £106m, with Mercia paying the council £22m in principal on the extended Facility B. At the end of the extension in 2029, the facility must either be refinanced or the plant reverts to the councils.
findings.matters: The £92m loan is a material long-term asset, but the extension to 2029 creates a cliff refinancing risk in 2028-29 when other borrowing pressures may be acute. The council should clarify its plan for what happens when the extension ends.
findings.figures: Loan carrying value: £92m as at 31 March 2024; extended unitary payment reduction: £2.5m upfront, £4.5m p.a. (2022-23), £6m p.a. (2024 onwards); bullet repayment reduced to £106m; Mercia to pay £22m principal
findings.quote: In partnership with Herefordshire County Council, the County Council provided finance to Mercia Waste for the building of an Energy from Waste Plant, which they are operating for a period determined by the existing PFI contract... Loans granted to Mercia Waste for this purpose will be considered separately to normal Treasury Management investment activity... As at the 31 March 2024, the carrying value of the loan to Mercia Waste was £92m

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4 - Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: Banking arrangements require the council to pay 4% over base rate on overdrafts while earning only base rate minus 75bp on deposits, creating a wide carry loss.
findings.detail: As of December 2025, the council's banking terms are: 4% over base rate on debit balances (overdraft), versus base rate minus 75 basis points on credit balances (deposits). With base rate at 4.00%, this means the council pays 8% on overdrafts while earning 3.25% on deposits. Given that the DSG position is forcing short-term borrowing, this spread is costly.
findings.matters: The 475bp spread between overdraft cost and deposit rate is wide and reflects weak negotiating position. With elevated debt levels, any reliance on overdraft facilities becomes expensive. A lender would want to see a renegotiation of these terms, particularly given the council's size.
findings.figures: Overdraft cost: base + 4% (= 8.00% at December 2025); deposit rate: base - 75bp (= 3.25% at December 2025); spread of 475bp
findings.quote: As at December 2025, Worcestershire County Council pays interest on the aggregate of the cleared debit balances at a rate of 4% over base rate and receives the base rate minus 75 basis points (BP) on the credit balance.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4 - Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: Capital financing requirement is forecast to grow 36% in four years (£731m to £997m), driven partly by £71.9m and £71m in assumed but unapproved Exceptional Financial Support.
findings.detail: The council's CFR is forecast to climb from £731.0m (2024/25) to £996.6m (2027/28). If EFS is not granted, actual borrowing needs would be lower but the council would face additional budget shortfalls.
findings.matters: The council is building multi-year budget projections on the assumption of unconfirmed government funding. If EFS is withheld or delayed, the council will face a shortfall requiring either further borrowing, service cuts, or reserve drawdown.
findings.figures: CFR grows from £731.0m (2024/25) to £996.6m (2027/28); EFS assumed at £71.9m (2026/27) and £71.0m (2027/28), totalling £142.9m over two years

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4 - Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: Including DSG, the council will be borrowing above its capital financing requirement (over-borrowed) from 2026/27 onwards.
findings.detail: Table 9 shows that excluding DSG, the council is properly under-borrowed with £130.2m headroom against its CFR. But including the DSG short-term borrowing, actual debt will exceed the CFR: 2026/27 debt of £964.7m against CFR of £873.7m, 2027/28 debt of £1,248.3m against CFR of £996.6m. This violates prudent borrowing principles because the borrowing is not matched to capital assets.
findings.matters: Over-borrowing against CFR indicates unsustainable debt levels and loss of control over borrowing ratios. A lender would be concerned that debt continues to grow after the government takes over DSG (2027/28 onwards debt forecast is still £1,225.3m).

findings.headline: DSG High Needs deficit is forcing unplanned short-term borrowing and eroding investment income by £7.5m annually until 2028.
findings.detail: The council lost £7.5m in treasury management income in 2025/26 due to DSG High Needs deficit cash flow. Additional short-term borrowing will continue until March 2028 when the government takes responsibility. The CFO notes the council would have met its balanced budget requirement 'if the Government funded SEND High Needs adequately', flagging this as a significant issue driven by government policy, not council overspend.
findings.matters: This represents forced borrowing outside the capital programme, reducing financial flexibility and increasing debt service costs. A lender would need to understand whether the council's deficit management plan survives once this £7.5m+ annual impact is removed.

findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement projected to grow from £731m to £997m over four years.

findings.paper_title: 5 Appendix 5 Worcestershire PF - Audit Findings Report 2024-25 - updated for IAS19 distribution 260925
findings.headline: Investment valuations show £4.3 million timing differences that remain unadjusted in the financial statements
findings.detail: The auditors identified £4.318m of unadjusted differences between investment valuations in the Fund's financial statements and valuation statements from third-party investment managers. The differences arose because some Level 3 investment balances were valued using 31 December 2024 capital/NAV statements rather than 31 March 2025 statements, as the later statements were not available at the time the accounts were prepared. This was recorded as an unadjusted misstatement but deemed not material to the overall financial statements.
findings.matters: While marked immaterial, a £4.3m valuation gap indicates timing and coordination issues in obtaining investment valuations, and the cumulative unadjusted misstatements (including prior year £10.6m) total £14.996m across two years.

findings.paper_title: 5 Appendix 5 Worcestershire PF - Audit Findings Report 2024-25 - updated for IAS19 distribution 260925
findings.headline: Contributions are not reviewed and authorised before posting to the ledger, creating reliance on manual post-entry controls
findings.detail: The auditors identified that contributions received by the pension fund are not reviewed and authorised before being posted to the ledger. Instead, the fund relies on a formula-driven contribution monitoring spreadsheet as a compensating control. Management acknowledges this is a system limitation and plans to integrate review and authorisation controls within the new financial system (implementation timeline not specified).
findings.matters: Lack of pre-posting authorization represents a control weakness in transaction processing that increases risk of error or fraud entering the accounts. The effectiveness of the compensating manual control depends on consistent spreadsheet review.
findings.figures: Not specified

findings.paper_title: 5 Appendix 5 Worcestershire PF - Audit Findings Report 2024-25 - updated for IAS19 distribution 260925
findings.headline: Virgin Media pension scheme ruling creates unquantified contingent liability for LGPS funds including Worcestershire
findings.detail: The High Court ruled in Virgin Media v NTL Pension Trustees that certain defined benefit pension scheme amendments were invalid without proper actuarial certification. The Court of Appeal upheld this in July 2024. HM Treasury and Government Actuaries Department are investigating whether similar certificates exist for LGPS amendments. Management has disclosed this as a contingent liability in the financial statements, but the impact is not yet quantifiable.
findings.matters: A material adverse ruling on LGPS scheme amendments could expose the fund to significant unfunded liabilities or restructuring costs, depending on the scope of certificates found to be deficient.
findings.figures: Impact not yet quantifiable; disclosed as contingent liability
findings.quote: As the impact of the ruling of the Virgin media case is not yet quantifiable, management has included a disclosure within the contingent liability note of the financial statements.

findings.paper_title: 5 Appendix 6 - WCC Interim Auditors Annual Report 2024-25
findings.headline: SEND service rated level 3 (widespread systemic failings) by Ofsted and CQC in April 2024 with two priority actions still outstanding
findings.detail: An Ofsted and CQC joint inspection of the council's SEND (Special Educational Needs and Disabilities) service in April 2024 resulted in a level 3 grading, reporting 'widespread and/or systemic failings'. Two priority actions were required of the local area partnership. The auditor made a key recommendation that the council work at pace with partners to deliver the SEND priority actions to the timescales required. This service is statutory, its costs are driving the DSG deficit crisis, and the systemic failings indicate control problems.
findings.matters: SEND is one of the council's largest budget pressures and the primary driver of its £184m DSG deficit projection. Systemic service failings increase the risk of escalating costs and potential regulatory intervention.

findings.paper_title: 5 Appendix 6 - WCC Interim Auditors Annual Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Performance management collapsed with no Cabinet reporting of corporate performance in 2024/25 or up to July 2025
findings.detail: The auditor found no corporate performance reporting to Cabinet in 2024/25, despite making an improvement recommendation in the prior year that the council enhance its performance monitoring arrangements. The council lacks a golden thread between its Corporate Plan and service delivery, 15 KPIs were not reviewed for three years, and performance reporting was only published on the website for 2023/24 until June 2025. The auditor identified this as a significant weakness because without performance management underpinned by robust data, the council cannot understand what improvements are needed.
findings.matters: Performance management is critical to effective financial control. The absence of regular performance reporting to senior decision-makers undermines the council's ability to identify problems early and make informed decisions about resource allocation and efficiency improvements.
findings.figures: Zero Cabinet performance reporting in 2024/25 and up to July 2025. 15 KPIs not reviewed for three years.
findings.quote: In 2024/25 and up to July 2025 the Cabinet saw no performance reporting. The Council has an insufficiently developed performance management framework with no golden thread in place between the Corporate Plan and Directorate and Service Plans

findings.paper_title: 5 Appendix 6 - WCC Interim Auditors Annual Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Long-term borrowing increased by £96.8m in a single year from £399.8m to £496.6m
findings.detail: The council's long-term borrowing rose from £399.8m on 31 March 2024 to £496.6m by 31 March 2025. Total long-term liabilities increased from £577.8m to £665.8m over the same period. This rapid increase in debt reflects the council's dependence on borrowing to fund its operations and capital programme, which adds to debt servicing costs and reduces financial flexibility.
findings.matters: A lender must assess debt sustainability. The pace and scale of borrowing growth, combined with the council's structural deficits and reserve depletion, raises questions about the council's ability to service and repay this debt.
findings.figures: Long-term borrowing increased from £399.8m to £496.6m (increase of £96.8m). Total long-term liabilities increased from £577.8m to £665.8m

findings.paper_title: 5 Appendix 6 - WCC Interim Auditors Annual Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Overspend on 2024/25 budget of £6.2m was met from planned reserves after the council had not delivered £10.8m in cost reductions
findings.detail: The 2024/25 outturn showed a net overspend of £6.2m on a £433.4m budget after using £7.9m of planned reserves. This came after the council failed to deliver £10.8m in planned savings. The auditor notes that the Senior Leadership Team and Chief Officers were instructed to find alternative savings when gaps emerged, but 'these did not materialise and the overspend was met from risk reserves'. This reveals both operational control weakness and reliance on reserves to cover budget misses.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council can hold its budget. Missing savings targets and absorbing overruns from reserves indicates control issues and reduces confidence in budget forecasting.
findings.figures: 2024/25 budget £433.35m (including £35m structural deficit), outturn overspend £6.2m, covered by £7.9m planned reserves
findings.quote: The Senior Leadership Team and Chief Officers were instructed in 2024/25 to find alternative, achievable savings proposals where there are current gaps in delivery. We note these did not materialise and the overspend was met from risk reserves.

findings.paper_title: 5 Appendix 6 - WCC Interim Auditors Annual Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Council is dependent on Exceptional Financial Support of £33.6m for 2025/26 and has requested £43.6m more for 2026/27, subject to external assurance review
findings.detail: The 2025/26 budget of £495.6m is supported by £15m of reserves and £33.6m from Exceptional Financial Support, which will be borrowed at an estimated cost of £15m and is subject to external assurance review later in 2025. The council has also requested £43.6m in EFS to support 2026/27 budget setting, which is yet to be agreed. This indicates structural financial dependency on government emergency support that cannot continue indefinitely.
findings.matters: A lender must assess the sustainability of EFS dependence. These are exceptional measures with conditions attached, and the government may not extend support indefinitely. The council needs to demonstrate a path to financial independence.

findings.paper_title: 5 Appendix 6 - WCC Interim Auditors Annual Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Savings programme is delivering only 72% of target with a budget gap of £48.6m filled by reserves and emergency government support
findings.detail: In 2024/25, the council set a savings target of £37.2m but delivered only £27.6m (72%), leaving £10.8m undelivered including £4.69m in corporate savings. For 2025/26, the council included only £12.51m of savings proposals to address a budget gap of £48.6m. The remaining gap is filled by £15m from reserves and £33.6m from Exceptional Financial Support. The auditor made a key recommendation that savings must address the gap at scale and pace.
findings.matters: The council is not delivering the operational efficiencies needed to stabilise its finances. Heavy reliance on one-off reserves and government bailout funding rather than sustainable savings is not a viable long-term position for a lender to support.
findings.figures: 2024/25 savings target £37.2m, delivered £27.6m (72%). 2025/26 budget gap £48.6m, addressed with £12.51m savings plus £15m reserves and £33.6m EFS
findings.quote: In 2024/25 the Council had a savings target of £37.2m and it delivered £27.6m (72%). Of the £10.8m undelivered savings £4.69m were corporate savings from areas such as the management review... The Council is not identifying and delivering savings in line with the scale of its budget requirements.

findings.paper_title: 5 Appendix 6 - WCC Interim Auditors Annual Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Earmarked risk reserves falling from £43.5m to £7.1m by March 2026 as the council uses them to fund services
findings.detail: The council's four main earmarked risk reserves had an opening balance of £43.5m on 1 April 2024, fell to £28.7m in 2024/25, and are expected to reach only £7.1m by 31 March 2026. The council has already committed £15m of these reserves to balance the 2025/26 budget and £1.875m for a County Hall decommissioning options appraisal. This continued draw on reserves to support service provision is described as unsustainable.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know that the council's financial buffer is collapsing. Reserves at this level offer minimal protection against unexpected shocks or service pressures.
findings.figures: Opening balance £43.5m (1 April 2024), reducing to £28.7m (31 March 2025), expected to be £7.1m (31 March 2026)
