findings.paper_title: 5 Appendix 6 - WCC Interim Auditors Annual Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant deficit has doubled in a year and will exceed £184m by March 2026 with no reserves to cover it after the statutory override ends in 2028
findings.detail: The DSG deficit jumped from £44.2m on 31 March 2024 to £98.2m on 31 March 2025 (87% increase) and is projected at £184.4m by 31 March 2026. The council has no reserves to accommodate this deficit if the statutory override is lifted on 31 March 2028. The auditor identified a significant weakness and issued a statutory recommendation requiring the council to urgently develop and agree a deficit management plan to begin reducing the deficit over time.
findings.matters: This is a structural solvency risk. If the override is not extended, the council becomes liable for a deficit roughly equivalent to its entire general fund balance and earmarked reserves combined, threatening financial sustainability.
findings.figures: DSG deficit £44.2m (31 March 2024), £98.2m (31 March 2025), projected £184.4m (31 March 2026). Council has no reserves to cover this.
findings.quote: The Council has no reserves to accommodate this deficit if the statutory override is lifted on 31 March 2028 this is a significant risk to its financial sustainability.

findings.paper_title: 7 Budget Monitoring P6 Final
findings.headline: Capital programme slippage of £50m in the first half year reduces 2025/26 spend from £209m to £159m, signalling either planning delays or financing constraints
findings.detail: The original 2025/26 capital budget approved in February was £209m. By Month 6, this has been reprofiled down to £159m (£125m excluding EFS funding), a recashflow of £50m. Major delayed schemes include: A38 Bromsgrove Phases 2-6 (£10.7m), Bromsgrove High 2FE expansion (£4.7m), Hampton Bridge (£4.5m), Bus Services Improvement Grant (£3m), Expansion to increase Special School Capacity (£3m). The report notes capital managers must prioritise 'early reporting of slippage'.
findings.matters: Large capital slippage suggests either: (a) the council cannot finance its own borrowing at the pace planned, or (b) projects are poorly scoped and delayed. Either is a red flag. The combination with revenue overspends suggests a council struggling to execute its strategy.
findings.figures: £50m recashflowed from 2025/26 to later years, 2025/26 budget fell from £209m to £159m (24% reduction), actuals YTD £39m (31% of revised £125m non-EFS budget)
findings.quote: By the end of Quarter 2, £50 million of forecast spend has been recashflowed from 2025/26 to subsequent years, with the most significant areas of re-cashflow being: A38 Bromsgrove Phases 2 to 6: £10.7 million, Bromsgrove High 2FE expansion: £4.7 million, Hampton Bridge: £4.5 million

findings.paper_title: 7 Budget Monitoring P6 Final
findings.headline: Government has delayed SEND reforms from autumn 2025 to 2026, leaving the DSG funding crisis unaddressed for at least another year
findings.detail: The government was expected to set out SEND reform approaches in a Schools White Paper in autumn 2025, but has now delayed this to 2026. The council explicitly states this is 'massively disappointing' because 'We need comprehensive changes that will make the system sustainable and address the dramatic rise in costs we have seen over the last decade.' Without reforms, the £193.7m DSG deficit this year will continue to mount unchecked. The council notes that 38 county and largest unitary authorities in England have accumulated 'unmanageable' SEND deficits.
findings.matters: The structural SEND funding crisis is not being addressed by central government. Every quarter the deficit grows with no policy solution in sight. This removes any hope of the council 'growing into' the problem.
findings.figures: EHCP spending in England forecast to reach £21bn by 2029 (double the 2016 level), one-in-twenty pupils under 16 now have EHCP (up from 2.7% a decade ago)
findings.quote: The recent announcement from Government on the delay setting out reforms to special educational needs and disabilities (SEND) services until 'early' in 2026 is massively disappointing. We need comprehensive changes that will make the system sustainable and address the dramatic rise in costs we have seen over the last decade.

findings.paper_title: 7 Budget Monitoring P6 Final
findings.headline: Revenue debt has grown to £41m with £6.6m in legal proceedings or litigation, indicating collection difficulties
findings.detail: Total council revenue debt at Period 6 is £41m, up from £37.7m in the same period last year (an increase of £3.3m or 8.7%). Of this, £6.6m is currently with Legal Services for review or in litigation. The report flags 'Debt recovery remains a key issue for the council' and the position is reported to members through Audit & Governance Committee.
findings.matters: Growing uncollectable debt signals either rising resident inability to pay (sign of local economic distress) or council ineffectiveness in recovery. £6.6m in litigation suggests disputes rather than straightforward arrears, which is harder to resolve.
findings.figures: £41m total revenue debt (up from £37.7m prior year same period, +£3.3m), £6.6m in legal review/litigation
findings.quote: Total council's revenue debt for Period 6 stands at £41 million. This is an increase when compared to the same period in 2024/25 when it was £37.7 million. Debt recovery remains a key issue for the council, with c£6.6 million of debt currently with Legal Services for review, or in litigation.

findings.paper_title: 7 Budget Monitoring P6 Final
findings.headline: The council is dependent on £33.6m of Exceptional Financial Support to balance 2025/26 and will need to request continuation for 2026/27 with a forecast gap of £63.7m
findings.detail: The 2025/26 budget could not be balanced without £33.6m of Exceptional Financial Support (EFS), a Capitalisation Direction from Government under the Local Government Act 2003. At Month 6, this remains in place as government support 'in principle'. For 2026/27, the estimated budget gap is £63.7m. The report states 'we expect to update Cabinet again in December, ahead of bringing forward final proposals for the 2026/27 budget' and flags that 'Even assuming a request is granted for a continuation of Exceptional Financial Support for 2026/27 and Council Tax increases, the Council will have to find significant further savings in 2026/27 from reducing spending and/or increasing income to avoid a S114 Notice.'
findings.matters: EFS is a temporary bridge, not a structural fix. The fact that it is already needed for 2026/27 and the gap is rising signals the council cannot find its own way to balance without either finding £63m+ in savings or requesting emergency support indefinitely.
findings.figures: £33.6m EFS in 2025/26 budget, £63.7m estimated gap for 2026/27
findings.quote: The 2025/26 budget could not be balanced without Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) of £33.6 million. Even assuming a request is granted for a continuation of Exceptional Financial Support for 2026/27 and Council Tax increases, the Council will have to find significant further savings in 2026/27 from reducing spending and/or increasing income to avoid a S114 Notice.

findings.paper_title: 7 Budget Monitoring P6 Final
findings.headline: Only 88% of the £12.5m savings programme is on track; £0.3m is rated red and unachievable this year including the Vale Lodge £763k saving
findings.detail: The council approved £12.5m in savings for 2025/26. As at Month 6, 88% (£11.1m) is rated green, of which 81% (£10.1m) has been achieved. However, 9% (£1.1m) is amber and 2% (£0.3m) is red. The red savings are in Children's Services: Vale Lodge review £763k (delayed pending Cabinet decision), Fostering Respite £127k, Expansion of Internal Supported Living £151k, Positive Outcomes Project review £30k. Directors are expected to identify alternative savings to mitigate non-delivery.
findings.matters: If 12% of planned savings slip, the overspend widens and the council needs larger reserve drawdowns or deeper cuts. The red-rated Vale Lodge saving suggests operational decisions are stalled, not just delayed.
findings.figures: £12.5m total savings target, 88% green (£11.1m), 81% achieved (£10.1m), 9% amber (£1.1m), 2% red (£0.3m). Vale Lodge £763k unachievable this year.
findings.quote: 88% currently rated green (£11.1 million) of which 81% (£10.1 million) has been achieved to date, 9% amber (£1.1 million) and 2% red (£0.3 million)

findings.paper_title: 7 Budget Monitoring P6 Final
findings.headline: Usable reserves are collapsing, falling from £93.7m (March 2025) to a forecast £72.5m (March 2026), with only £19.6m of that being genuinely unrestricted risk reserves
findings.detail: Opening Earmarked Reserves were £93.7m. The council expects to draw down £21.2m this year, leaving £72.5m. However, of that closing balance, only £19.6m is classified as usable 'unearmarked' risk reserve (Finance Risk Reserve, Business Rates Retention, Transformation Reserve). The remainder is either ring-fenced to grants/health, schools, insurance, or commitments. The General Fund Balance is £19.2m (4.4% of budget) but the Section 151 Officer states it should be minimum 5% (£21.7m). The council is currently using £11.3m of reserves just to balance 2025/26. External Auditors have given a Key Recommendation to agree a reserves replenishment plan.
findings.matters: A council with £19.6m of liquid reserves to handle emergencies or service shocks is dangerously exposed. The target 5% buffer is considered minimum; Worcestershire is below it and falling. This severely constrains the council's ability to manage any adverse variance or demand spike.
findings.figures: Opening reserves £93.7m, closing forecast £72.5m, usable risk reserves only £19.6m (down from £28.7m March 2025), General Fund Balance £19.2m (4.4% of budget vs 5% target of £21.7m), £11.3m reserves drawn in 2025/26
findings.quote: The value of the Council's Earmarked reserves was £93.7 million, however this includes several ring-fenced grant related reserves. A total of £21.2 million of reserves are expected to be drawn down this year, leaving a forecast closing balance of £72.5 million. Of the £72.5 million forecast to be remaining at the year end, only c£19.6 million is deemed to be usable and unearmarked.

findings.paper_title: 7 Budget Monitoring P6 Final
findings.headline: The Dedicated Schools Grant High Needs deficit will rise from £98.2m to £193.7m in one year and will crystallize as a budget hit when the statutory override expires in March 2028
findings.detail: The DSG High Needs deficit opened at £98.2m (March 2025) and is forecast to reach £193.7m by year-end. The number of children with EHCPs has increased 2.75% in Q2 alone (to 7,806) and is up 20% year-on-year from 6,530. The statutory override allowing DSG deficits to sit off the main balance sheet expires March 2028. At that point, the forecast deficit will be approximately £322.2m and will hit the council's main revenue budget unless government provides additional funding. The External Auditor has issued a Statutory Recommendation on DSG management.
findings.matters: This is the single largest threat to Worcestershire's solvency. When the override expires, the council will either need to find £322m from reserves (which do not exist) or from additional cuts and savings that dwarf anything currently planned. Without reform to SEND funding, this is unavoidable.
findings.figures: Opening DSG deficit £98.2m (March 2025), forecast year-end £193.7m, forecast at March 2028 approximately £322.2m, EHCPs up 2.75% in Q2 to 7,806, up 20% year-on-year from 6,530
findings.quote: The accumulated deficit position for the DSG reserves at 1 April 2025 was a deficit balance of £98.2 million, built up from previous years overspends. Considering the current forecast for 2025/26, the deficit balance is expected to increase to £193.7 million at year-end

findings.paper_title: 7 Budget Monitoring P6 Final
findings.headline: Looked After Children external placements have risen 7% in a year with unit costs jumping 7-12%, driving an £8.1m overspend
findings.detail: External LAC placements are now 671 (September 2025) versus 651 in September 2024, a 7% annual increase. Agency Residential placements rose from 162 to 169 (+7 children) while unit cost jumped from £6,563/week to £7,123/week (+8.5%). Independent Fostering placements up 8 to 360 with unit cost rising from £1,000 to £1,055/week (+5.5%). Forecast overspend in Children's Services is £8.1m on a net budget of £107.3m.
findings.matters: Rising external LAC placements are sticky and expensive; the council is moving toward more costly residential care and cannot control unit prices set by private providers. This is symptomatic of a unable-to-manage social care system, not a temporary fluctuation.
findings.figures: External placements 671 (+20 in year = 7% increase), Agency Residential unit cost £6,563→£7,123/week, Independent Fostering £1,000→£1,055/week, 4% total LAC growth (1,035→1,071), forecast overspend £8.1m on £107.3m
findings.quote: the current demographic pressures in placements for Looked After Children and high inflation in care placements, which is a volatile area of forecasting. This is despite the recurrent budget being amended and growth and contract inflation being applied in 2025/26.

findings.paper_title: 7 Budget Monitoring P6 Final
findings.headline: Adult Social Care placement demand is rising faster than any prior year, with unit costs inflating 6-16% above budget
findings.detail: Since March 2025, Adult Services have taken on 165 net new care packages (2.3% growth) versus 0.4% in the same period last year. Unit costs are rising well above inflation: Physical Disability Residential +12% (£157/person/week), Learning Disability Residential +6.7% (£149/person/week), Mental Health Residential +6.7% (£84/person/week). The service forecasts a £10.2m overspend on placements before mitigation, with total Adult Services overspend at £8.3m against a net budget of £173.9m.
findings.matters: Demand-driven cost pressures in social care are a leading indicator of a council losing control of its largest budget area. Placement cost inflation above general CPI signals either market stress or the council accepting unprofitable contracts. This is recurring, not one-off.
findings.figures: 165 net new packages (2.3% six-month growth vs 0.4% prior year), unit costs +12% in Physical Disability Residential, +6.7% Learning Disability, +6.7% Mental Health, forecast overspend £8.3m on £173.9m budget
findings.quote: For the past four financial years placement activity and the unit cost of providing care has been higher than forecast despite the recurrent budget being amended and significant growth and contract inflation being applied to the budget. Demand has continued to rise in the first half year of 2025/26 and at a higher pace than the same period in 2024/25.

findings.paper_title: 7 Budget Monitoring P6 Final
findings.headline: The council is at risk of issuing a Section 114 notice and needs to avoid it by continuous focus on financial management
findings.detail: The Council explicitly confirms in its recommendations that it 'needs to continue to demonstrate its commitment to avoid the need to issue a Section 114 notice in 2025/26'. A Section 114 notice is a formal declaration that the council faces insolvency. The Section 25 Statement already highlighted risks of needing one given the MTFP forecast and reducing reserves, though a programme of activities has commenced.
findings.matters: A Section 114 notice would trigger severe restrictions on spending and governance, making the council unmortgageable and signalling imminent service collapse to lenders and investors.
findings.figures: £33.6m Exceptional Financial Support required just to balance 2025/26; £63.7m estimated gap for 2026/27
findings.quote: confirms that the whole Council needs to continue to demonstrate its commitment to avoid the need to issue a Section 114 notice in 2025/26 by continuous focus of financial management actions to reduce the forecast overspend

findings.paper_title: 2025 11 06 Interim Auditors Annual Report - App - WCC Interim Auditors Annual Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Reform party took minority administration in May 2025 with 27 of 57 councillors, and council is developing a Local Government Reorganisation Business Case with November 2025 timescale.
findings.detail: Worcestershire held elections in May 2025. Reform secured a minority administration with 27 elected councillors. The council is 'currently developing the Local Government Reorganisation Business Case for the November 2025 timescale.' LGR (merger with Herefordshire) is a significant structural change. A minority administration during a period of severe budget pressure and an LGR process creates governance uncertainty. The recovery plan the council needs to deliver may be overtaken by LGR.
findings.matters: LGR is a major structural change whose terms, cost, and staffing implications are unknown. It could distract from the urgent deficit and DSG recovery work, or alternatively could provide a reset opportunity. Lenders need clarity on whether the council's recovery plan is independent of LGR assumptions.
findings.figures: Reform secured minority administration: 27 of 57 councillors (May 2025). LGR Business Case due November 2025.
findings.quote: The Council is currently developing the Local Government Reorganisation Business Case for the November 2025 timescale. The most recent elections were in May 2025 when Reform secured a minority administration with 27 elected councillors.

findings.paper_title: 2025 11 06 Interim Auditors Annual Report - App - WCC Interim Auditors Annual Report 2024-25
findings.headline: No performance reporting to Cabinet in 2024/25 — performance management framework is insufficiently developed with no 'golden thread' to corporate plan.
findings.detail: The auditor found that 'In 2024/25 and up to July 2025 the Cabinet saw no performance reporting.' The council lacks 'a golden thread in place between the Corporate Plan and Directorate and Service Plans, Financial plans' and 'performance, risk and financial planning are not aligned.' The auditor raised key recommendation KR3 requiring the council to 'significantly improve performance management' and align reporting. This represents a governance failure — the council cannot demonstrate that it is executing its strategy or that services are improving.
findings.matters: If a council's leadership is not seeing performance data, they cannot make informed decisions about where to cut. This is the governance failure underlying the savings shortfalls and budget overruns.
findings.figures: No performance reporting to Cabinet in 2024/25. 15 KPIs were not reviewed for three years.
findings.quote: In 2024/25 and up to July 2025 the Cabinet saw no performance reporting... There is an insufficiently developed performance management framework with no golden thread in place between the Corporate Plan and Directorate and Service Plans, Financial plans

findings.paper_title: 2025 11 06 Interim Auditors Annual Report - App - WCC Interim Auditors Annual Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Medium-term financial strategy lacks substance — auditor expects 'significantly more detail and modelling' and a clearer link to corporate plan.
findings.detail: The council has a three-year medium-term financial strategy (MTFS) but the auditor states 'This has limited information. We would expect to see a robust MTFS with significantly more detail and modelling and a demonstratable link to the corporate plan.' This was included in key recommendation KR1 on financial planning and control. A weak MTFS indicates the council lacks a credible plan for managing the deficits identified in this report.
findings.matters: Without a detailed, credible MTFS the council has no tested plan for achieving sustainability. Lenders need to see a multi-year recovery trajectory with confidence intervals.
findings.figures: Council MTFS covers three-year period but is described as having 'limited information'.
findings.quote: The Council has a medium-term financial strategy (MTFS) that covers a three-year period. This has limited information. We would expect to see a robust MTFS with significantly more detail and modelling and a demonstratable link to the corporate plan.

findings.paper_title: 2025 11 06 Interim Auditors Annual Report - App - WCC Interim Auditors Annual Report 2024-25
findings.headline: 2024/25 revenue outturn was a net overspend of £6.2m after using £7.9m of planned reserves, with ongoing pressures in adults and children's social care and home to school transport.
findings.detail: Despite a net budget of £433.35m (including a structural deficit of £35m), the council overspent by £6.2m in 2024/25. This overspend was funded from reserves. The auditor notes 'Pressures continue in adults and children's social care and home to school transport.' These are statutory services with demand-driven costs. The council's financial controls enabled mitigation in the last quarter of the year, but the baseline position is unaffordable.
findings.matters: Overspending on demand-led services (adults social care, children's social care, home-to-school transport) indicates the council has not right-sized services to available funding. These are the highest-cost and least controllable parts of the budget.
findings.figures: 2024/25 net budget requirement £433.351m including structural deficit £35m. Outturn: net overspend £6.2m after using £7.9m planned reserves. Pressures in adults and children's social care, home to school transport.
findings.quote: The 2024/25 outturn was a net overspend of £6.2m after using £7.9m of planned reserves... Pressures continue in adults and children's social care and home to school transport.

findings.paper_title: 2025 11 06 Interim Auditors Annual Report - App - WCC Interim Auditors Annual Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Ofsted and CQC inspection of SEND rated the council level 3 ('widespread and/or systemic failings') with mandatory priority actions due by unspecified Ofsted/CQC timescales.
findings.detail: An Ofsted and CQC joint inspection of SEND was carried out in April 2024 and published 15 July 2024 with a level 3 grading, the lowest possible rating, reporting 'widespread and/or systemic failings'. The auditor made a key recommendation (KR4) that 'The Council should work at pace with partners to ensure the SEND priority actions are delivered to the timescales required by Ofsted and the CQC.' The council's SEND strategy covers £30.1m of investment over three years and involves weekly meetings, monthly committee meetings, and a new independent chair appointed in February 2025. However, a level 3 inspection is a regulatory failure and signals possible future intervention.
findings.matters: A level 3 SEND inspection means the council has failed to meet statutory duties in a high-cost, high-visibility area (education and disability support). Regulators may intervene. SEND costs are also driving the DSG deficit crisis. Failure in SEND signals failure in financial management.
findings.figures: SEND priority action plan dated September 2024, includes actions up to March 2026. Sufficiency planning: £30.1 million investment over 3 years. DSG deficit in High Needs block: £98.2m as at 31 March 2025.
findings.quote: Ofsted and CQC inspection of SEND was carried out in April 2024 and published on 15 July 2024. It was a level 3 grading reporting 'widespread and/ or systemic failings' in the SEND service.

findings.paper_title: 2025 11 06 Interim Auditors Annual Report - App - WCC Interim Auditors Annual Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Long-term borrowing increased by £96.8m in one year (from £399.8m to £496.6m) while long-term liabilities rose by £88m.
findings.detail: The council's long-term borrowing increased from £399.8m on 31 March 2024 to £496.6m on 31 March 2025. Total long-term liabilities increased from £577.8m to £665.8m over the same period. This is a material increase in debt during a period when the council is also drawing on reserves and requesting exceptional government support. Combined with the DSG deficit (which does not yet appear on the balance sheet but will when the override ends), this indicates escalating liabilities.
findings.matters: Rising debt while reserves deplete and savings targets are missed is a trajectory toward insolvency. The council's ability to service new debt becomes questionable if operating deficits persist.
findings.figures: Long-term borrowing: £399.8m (31 March 2024) to £496.6m (31 March 2025), increase of £96.8m. Total long-term liabilities: £577.8m to £665.8m, increase of £88m.
findings.quote: The Council's long-term borrowing increased from £399.8m on 31 March 2024 to £496.6m by 31 March 2025. Total long-term liabilities increased from £577.8m to £665.8m over this period.

findings.paper_title: 2025 11 06 Interim Auditors Annual Report - App - WCC Interim Auditors Annual Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Budget gap of £48.6m in 2025/26 filled by £15m reserves drawdown and £33.6m Exceptional Financial Support, with £43.6m EFS requested but not yet agreed for 2026/27.
findings.detail: The 2025/26 net budget is £495.6m. The council is dependent on £15m of reserves and £33.6m of EFS (borrowed at estimated £15m cost) to balance the budget. The council has also requested £43.6m to support 2026/27 budget setting, which has not yet been agreed. The auditor notes that EFS is 'subject to an external assurance review later in 2025'. This is structural dependency on exceptional government support; it is not sustainable and is conditional on government approval.
findings.matters: A council dependent on government bailout funding for two years running signals it has lost financial autonomy. Continued EFS dependency past 2026/27 would be unusual and signal political concerns beyond normal auditor interest.
findings.figures: 2025/26 budget £495.6m supported by £15m reserves + £33.6m EFS. 2026/27 requesting £43.6m EFS (not yet agreed). EFS is borrowed at estimated cost of £15m.
findings.quote: The 2025/26 net budget is £495.6m for 2025/26 supported by £15m of the risk reserves and £33.6m from Exceptional Financial Support (EFS). The Council also requested £43.6m to support 2026/27 budget setting.

findings.paper_title: 2025 11 06 Interim Auditors Annual Report - App - WCC Interim Auditors Annual Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Savings programme delivering only 72% of target — £10.8m unachieved in a year when £37.2m was required.
findings.detail: In 2024/25 the council set a savings target of £37.2m and delivered £27.6m (72%). Of the £10.8m shortfall, £4.69m were corporate savings from areas such as the management review. The auditor notes 'The Senior Leadership Team and Chief Officers were instructed in 2024/25 to find alternative, achievable savings proposals where there are current gaps in delivery. We note these did not materialise and the overspend was met from risk reserves.' This represents a deteriorating track record: 94% achieved in 2022/23, 78% in 2023/24, 72% in 2024/25. The 2025/26 budget proposes only £12.51m of new savings against a budget gap of £48.6m.
findings.matters: A council that cannot deliver half its planned savings and is falling behind year-on-year cannot be relied upon to execute a recovery plan. Lenders need credible delivery to justify future lending.
findings.figures: 2024/25: target £37.2m, delivered £27.6m (72%), shortfall £10.8m. 2025/26: proposals £12.51m against budget gap £48.6m. Declining achievement: 94% (2022/23), 78% (2023/24), 72% (2024/25).
findings.quote: In 2024/25 the Council had a savings target of £37.2m and it delivered £27.6m (72%). Of the £10.8m undelivered savings £4.69m were corporate savings from areas such as the management review. The Senior Leadership Team and Chief Officers were instructed in 2024/25 to find alternative, achievable savings proposals where there are current gaps in delivery. We note these did not materialise and the overspend was met from risk reserves.

findings.paper_title: 2025 11 06 Interim Auditors Annual Report - App - WCC Interim Auditors Annual Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Earmarked reserves depleting from £43.5m to projected £7.1m in two years — unsustainable draw-down to support current spending.
findings.detail: Earmarked risk reserves opened 2024/25 at £43.5m, reduced to £28.7m by outturn, and are expected to fall to £7.1m by 31 March 2026. The auditor explicitly states this 'continued use of reserves and balances to support service provision is not sustainable' and made a key recommendation (KR1) that the council 'work at pace to address its significant budget pressures and reduce reliance on EFS and its very limited reserves and agree a reserves replenishment plan'. Additionally £1.875m was drawn for a County Hall decommissioning options appraisal.
findings.matters: A council drawing reserves at this pace to fund operations is insolvent on a cash basis and will have no buffer for unexpected demand. This is the financial position of a council in severe distress.
findings.figures: Opening balance £43.5m (1 April 2024), reduced to £28.7m (31 March 2025), projected £7.1m (31 March 2026). General Fund balance increased from £16.1m to £19.2m but is less than 5% of net budget requirement.
findings.quote: The Council also has four earmarked risk reserves, with an opening balance of £43.5m which reduced to £28.7m in 2024/25 and are expected to decrease to £7.1m by 31 March 2026, this continued use of reserves and balances to support service provision is not sustainable.

findings.paper_title: 2025 11 06 Interim Auditors Annual Report - App - WCC Interim Auditors Annual Report 2024-25
findings.headline: High Needs DSG deficit doubled in one year to £98.2m with no credible plan to contain it before the statutory override ends in March 2028.
findings.detail: The DSG deficit increased from £44.2m (March 2024) to £98.2m (March 2025) and is projected to reach £184.4m by March 2026. The auditors note the council has 'no reserves to accommodate this deficit if the statutory override is lifted on 31 March 2028' and issued a statutory recommendation (SR1) that the council 'urgently address its increasing DSG deficit and work at pace, with its partners, to develop and agree a deficit management plan'. The council is an outlier among peer councils for the pace of deficit growth.
findings.matters: A lender cannot lend to a council if it becomes liable for a £184m deficit when government protection expires. This is existential financial risk with a hard 2028 deadline.
findings.figures: DSG deficit: £44.2m (2024), £98.2m (2025), projected £184.4m (2026). Annual increase: 87% in 2025. A business plan dated August 2025 identified only £3m of 'cost avoidance' against a deficit of this magnitude.
findings.quote: The Council has no reserves to accommodate this deficit if the statutory override is lifted on 31 March 2028 this is a significant risk to its financial sustainability.

findings.paper_title: 2025 11 06 Interim Auditors Annual Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Auditor issued statutory recommendation to urgently address Worcestershire's increasing Dedicated Schools Grant deficit.
findings.detail: Grant Thornton has formally recommended that the Council urgently address its increasing DSG deficit and develop a deficit management plan to reduce it over time. The Council has established a High Needs Dedicated Schools Grant Deficit Management Group meeting fortnightly, with the Chief Finance Officer and Director of Children's Services joining monthly. Clear workstreams with senior leadership owners are targeting cost avoidance and deficit reduction, with progress reported quarterly to SLT, monthly to SEND Partnership Committee, and regularly to Children's Overview and Scrutiny Committee.
findings.matters: A statutory audit recommendation signals a significant weakness in council arrangements; an increasing DSG deficit is a structural funding problem that constrains available resources and affects the council's financial sustainability and borrowing capacity.
findings.figures: DSG deficit amount not stated in document extract
findings.quote: The Council should urgently address its increasing DSG deficit and work at pace, with its partners, to develop and agree a deficit management plan to begin to reduce the deficit over time.

findings.paper_title: au2025 09 25 External Audit PF AFR - Audit Findings Report 2024-25 Final
findings.headline: Contribution transactions are not automatically reviewed and authorised before posting to the financial ledger
findings.detail: The E5 financial system does not support automated review and authorisation of pension contributions. Manual authorisation is in place but not documented as a formal control. The fund lacks a system-enforced control over one of its largest transaction streams. Management acknowledges this as a system limitation and has specified automated authorization in the new financial system design.
findings.matters: Lack of automated controls over contributions (a primary fund cash inflow) increases the risk of undetected error or processing failure.
findings.figures: Not specified; contributions are a major fund account flow
findings.quote: Contributions received are not reviewed and authorised before being posted to the ledger. However, the contribution monitoring spreadsheet is formula-driven highlights and the current E5 financial system does not support automated review and authorisation of contributions, requiring a manual process outside the system.

findings.paper_title: au2025 09 25 External Audit PF AFR - Audit Findings Report 2024-25 Final
findings.headline: Level 3 investment valuations contain £4.3m of unadjusted timing differences and carry forward £10.6m from prior year
findings.detail: The fund's £1,152.9m in Level 3 investments (property, infrastructure, debt funds) are valued based on unobservable inputs. Some December 2024 valuations were used because 31 March 2025 statements were not available, creating £4.3m of under-statement. A further £10.6m of unadjusted differences from the prior year remain outstanding. These were deemed not material but indicate ongoing valuation judgment challenges.
findings.matters: Accumulated valuation differences in illiquid assets suggest potential volatility in reported fund values and understatement of actual assets.
findings.figures: £4.3m current year unadjusted difference; £10.6m prior year difference; £1,152.9m total Level 3 investments
findings.quote: We have noted a £4.3m under-statement in respect of the valuation of level 3 investments due to timing differences as some of the investment balances are based on 31 December 2024 capital / NAV statements as these were the latest available at the date of producing the financial statements.

findings.paper_title: au2025 09 25 External Audit PF AFR - Audit Findings Report 2024-25 Final
findings.headline: Virgin Media pension case has created an unquantified contingent liability for the LGPS
findings.detail: The Court of Appeal upheld a High Court ruling (Virgin Media v NTL) that certain defined benefit pension scheme amendments were invalid without proper actuarial certification. HM Treasury is investigating whether equivalent certificates exist for LGPS prior amendments. No impact is yet quantifiable but a disclosure has been added to the fund's contingent liabilities.

news_drafts.headline: Worcestershire council gets £33.6m aid but auditors warn it increases debt for 20 years
news_drafts.lead: Worcestershire County Council has received £33.6 million in Exceptional Financial Support from government to help balance its 2025-26 budget. But the external auditor has warned members that this support "represents a structural increase to the Authority's debt position rather than a one-off adjustment." The money was granted as a capitalisation direction—government permission to treat day-to-day spending as capital spending so it can be borrowed—which requires the council to repay it over time. The council's minimum revenue provision, the amount it must set aside each year to repay borrowing, has increased by £1.2 million to £18.4 million for 2025-26, with charges continuing for up to 20 years. Grant Thornton identified significant weaknesses in the council's financial sustainability and retained key recommendations from the previous year requiring urgent action.
